summary_html: **Healthcare encounters** that reveal suspected abuse or neglect trigger reporting obligations. Federal law governs mandatory reporting in federal facilities and coordination with state systems.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — state reporter systems and protections  
- **Victims of Child Abuse Act (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20307)** — mandates in federal settings, CAC coordination

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Dawn Farrell v. Warren County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination of the mother's rights to all three children under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the statutory definitions of an abused or neglected child do not require proof of actual harm to each child and that abuse of a sibling plus an unsafe home environment supports the finding as to the others.
key_cases.relevance: The case originated in a hospital's findings of non-accidental trauma to an infant, the paradigm medical disclosure that opens a Virginia CPS case.
key_cases.quote: Thus, we hold that the evidence was sufficient to support the trial court’s determination that E. and W. were abused or neglected.

key_cases.case_name: Christopher Farrell v. Warren County Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination and rejected the father's due process challenge, holding that Code § 16.1-283(B) is constitutional because the Department must prove every element supporting termination by clear and convincing evidence even though the underlying abuse or neglect adjudication uses a preponderance standard.
key_cases.relevance: The medical evidence of the infant's injuries drove the adjudication, and the father's challenge to the standard of proof applied to it was rejected.
key_cases.quote: In the context of terminating a parent’s rights, the Due Process Clause requires that the Department prove each of the necessary allegations of parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.case_name: Adam Yafi v. Stafford Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(E), holding that where a parent is convicted of felony child abuse causing serious bodily injury to a sibling or subjects a child to aggravated circumstances, the Department need not prove it offered reasonable and appropriate rehabilitative services.
key_cases.relevance: The case arose from a half-sibling's hospitalization for serious bodily injury, the medical disclosure pathway into a Virginia abuse case.
key_cases.quote: the termination of Yafi’s residual parental rights under Code § 16.1-283(E)(iii) and 16.1-283(E)(iv) did not require a predicate showing that DSS provided any services to Yafi

key_cases.case_name: Jenkins v. Winchester Department of Social Services
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed both an abuse-and-neglect finding as to a newborn removed days after birth and the termination of the mother's rights to an older child, holding that the statutory definitions require no proof of harm already suffered because 'substantial risk' speaks prospectively and Code § 16.1-251(A)(1) contemplates removal before the child enters the dangerous environment.
key_cases.relevance: The Department filed its petition the day after the child's birth at the Winchester Medical Center based on its prior experience with the mother, the paradigm hospital-based opening of a Virginia case on a newborn.
key_cases.quote: We agree with the Department that the statutory definitions of an abused or neglected child do not require proof of actual harm or impairment having been experienced by the child.

mandatory_reporters: Designated professionals only — Virginia is NOT a universal-reporter state (Va. Code § 63.2-1509(A))
Any person licensed to practice medicine or any of the healing arts
Any hospital resident or intern, and any person employed in the nursing profession
Any person employed as a social worker or family-services specialist
Any probation officer
Any teacher or other person employed in a public or private school, kindergarten, or child day program (§ 22.1-289.02)
Any person providing full-time or part-time child care for pay on a regularly planned basis
Any mental health professional
Any law-enforcement officer or animal control officer
Any mediator eligible to receive court referrals (§ 8.01-576.8)
Any professional staff person employed by a private or state-operated hospital, institution, or facility to which children have been committed or placed for care and treatment
Any person 18 or older associated with or employed by any public or private organization responsible for the care, custody, or control of children
Any court-appointed special advocate (CASA) designated under § 9.1-151 et seq.
Any person 18 or older who has received Department of Social Services-approved training in recognizing and reporting child abuse and neglect
Any local department employee who determines eligibility for public assistance
Any emergency medical services provider certified by the Board of Health (§ 32.1-111.5)
Any athletic coach, director, or other person 18 or older employed by or volunteering with a public or private sports organization or team, or a school athletics program
Administrators or employees 18 or older of public or private day camps, youth centers, and youth recreation programs
Any person employed by a public or private institution of higher education, other than an attorney providing legal representation to a client
Any minister, priest, rabbi, imam, or duly accredited practitioner of a religious organization, subject to the clergy-privilege exceptions in § 63.2-1509(A)(19)
Any person who engages in the practice of behavior analysis (§ 54.1-2900)

timeline_requirements.deadline: Face-to-face contact within the response time set at intake; within 24 hours if the child is under 2
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Worker must document in writing why the contact or observation was not made (22VAC40-705-80)

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days (extendable to a total of 60 days on written justification, or to 90 days in a joint law-enforcement investigation)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute sets no penalty; any extension requires written justification and the local department must notify the alleged abuser or neglector and the child's parents (Va. Code § 63.2-1505(B)(5); 22VAC40-705-120)
